To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the sensitivity of laboratory and field tests was comparable, that the AF and SSD methods were equally protective and that measured concentrations of LAS and TBT exceeded calculated PNECs, indicating a potential risk to ecosystems.

Measured effect concentrations of TBT and LAS on single, individual endpoints in field experiments are comparable to those obtained in laboratory tests and are sufficient to extrapolate toxicant effects to the ecosystem level."

1) structural parameters were more often sensitive than functional ones; 2) measured effect concentrations covered approximately same range between laboratory experiments and field experiments; 3) both SSD and AF approaches were able to produce PNECs that were protective for ecosystems; 4) AF approach is simpler than SSD models and results PNECs which are no less conservative than SSD; 5) calculated PNEC values were lower than measured EC values for both substances and therefore, they may pose a threat
In summary, our research is concerned with
the extrapolation of ecotoxicological data between different endpoints, between laboratory and field, and between different scales.
the question of whether single-species laboratory tests provide reliable information on effects at the ecosystem-level.
the question of how to extrapolate toxicant effects from single, individual-level effect endpoints to the ecosystem level.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
both laboratory and field tests are useful to assess the potential risks of chemicals to aquatic organisms.
the AF approach is a simple but effective tool to extrapolate laboratory data for environmental risk assessment.
the laboratory data are not necessarily more conservative than the field data.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of laboratory toxicity tests is a good starting point for risk assessment, but that the results should be evaluated and refined by field studies and/or by using more complex SSD models.
the AF approach can be used as an alternative to SSD models for PNEC calculations.
the extrapolation of laboratory data to the field is possible and that the AF approach is a useful tool for risk assessment of chemicals in marine ecosystems.
The main takeaway from our work is that
extrapolation methods are useful for assessing risk of chemicals to marine organisms, and they can be used with confidence to provide guidance on chemical risk assessment.

laboratory single-species toxicity tests can be used for risk assessment of chemicals in marine systems, provided that the appropriate effect endpoints are selected and that the PNEC values are calculated with a conservative approach.
the AF approach can be used to derive PNECs for substances with limited ecotoxicological data.
